# Chapter Seven: Day 91

The embargo expired at 9:00 a.m. Eastern. Mara had been awake since 4:40, watching the ceiling of her rented apartment in Arlington, running the timeline one more time.

Ninety days. She'd given Meridian Systems ninety days, and for eighty-seven of them, they'd done everything right. Acknowledged the report within six hours. Assigned a tracker. Flown her out to Reston in February, put her in a glass conference room with a view of the parking lot, and let her explain — patiently, twice — how their firmware update pipeline accepted signed manifests from a staging domain that shared a TLS certificate with production. One misconfigured CNAME, she'd told them, and anyone who could poison DNS could push a malicious update to every Meridian-managed device in North America. Hospitals. Water utilities. Three of the five largest school districts in the country.

They'd believed her. That was the part she kept coming back to. The VP of engineering, a tired man named Okafor with a handshake like a vice, had said *you're right, we checked, you're right* before she'd finished her second slide. Most vendors fought. Meridian had simply gone pale.

Then, on day 88, the silence started.

Her contact — a PR person named Dev, who was clearly standing in front of a mirror practicing the word *transparency* — had gone from answering emails in twenty minutes to answering nothing. The advisory page that was supposed to publish at 9:00 this morning still showed a 404. And at 6:12 a.m., a message had arrived from an address she didn't recognize, no subject line, four words:

**"Delay it. Everyone wins."**

She'd screenshotted it, hashed the file, and emailed both to her lawyer before her coffee finished brewing. Then she'd done the thing she was actually trained to do: she'd checked whether the message was a bluff.

It wasn't. That was the problem. A bluff implies someone thinks you can be moved. This read more like a courtesy — the way you notify a neighbor before the demolition crew arrives. Someone at Meridian, or above Meridian, had decided that a public advisory describing a DNS-based update hijack was more dangerous than the fix being incomplete. And they were right, in the narrow sense. The patch had shipped to 60% of the fleet. The other 40% — the legacy gateways, the ones running the old manifest parser — were still exposed, and would be for another six weeks, because the carrier certification cycle for their firmware was glacial and nobody had planned for that.

Mara understood the arithmetic. She'd spent eleven years in this business precisely because she understood arithmetic like that. Six weeks of exposure to forty million devices, versus six weeks of exposure plus a public document telling every attacker on earth exactly where the soft spot was.

She also understood what happened to companies that quietly decided the arithmetic for everyone.

At 8:15, she called Okafor directly — the number he'd given her in February with the words *if anything ever goes sideways*. It rang four times.

"It's not what you think," he said, instead of hello.

"Then tell me what it is."

"The carrier cert slipped. Dev's team is rewriting the advisory language to lead with the mitigation instead of the vulnerability. It's not suppression, it's sequencing. We asked for seventy-two hours."

"Nobody asked me for seventy-two hours. The window closed at nine. The agreement says I publish independently if the advisory isn't live."

"I know what the agreement says." A pause, and then, quieter, the sound of a man choosing honesty over his career: "There's also pressure from above my head that I don't fully understand. Someone flagged the advisory draft to legal at the parent level. I found out because my own draft came back redlined by people I've never met."

Mara closed her eyes. "Okafor. Is the fix deployed or not?"

"Sixty percent. The rest is real and it's real slow."

"Then here's what happens. At nine-oh-one, I publish. Full technical detail, the CNAME, the certificate overlap, the affected SKUs, and the exact mitigation status per SKU — including the forty percent that isn't patched. I'm not going to let them pretend it's done, and I'm not going to let anyone pretend it's secret. Operators can protect themselves only if they know both halves."

"You'll cause the thing you're trying to prevent."

"No. Silence causes it. An attacker finds this stuff eventually — that's the whole job. The only variable is whether the defenders find out first." She looked at the clock. 8:51. "You have nine minutes to get the advisory up yourselves. I'd rather link to yours."
